findings.where: Desktop hero: the sheet's first screen, from the title block down through the section drawing to the name, the blurb and WRITE TO MARK
findings.fault: The title block and the drawing with its dimension lines take about 650 px of height before any words appear. In the 900 px shot the name starts at about 660 px and the only button sits about 30 px above the fold. On a shorter laptop window the name is cut at the fold and the button falls below it, so the first screen is a drawing with no name and no way to get in touch. The brief wants the picture first, but it also wants Mark and the one action reachable once the picture has had its moment. This layout gives no room for either on a short screen.
findings.who_objects: Development-bank staff who often browse on 1366×768 corporate laptops. Their first screen would show a blueprint with no name, no line and no action, and they would have to scroll to learn whose sheet it is.

findings.where: Phone hero: the section drawing above MARK M. MOSELEY
findings.fault: At 390 px the drawing that leads the desktop page shrinks to a strip about 130 px tall under a 115 px title block. The name, role lines, blurb and amber button then fill the rest of the first screen. Text wins the phone view, and the calm picture-first moment, which is the main idea of this direction, is lost.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose brief puts calm first, with one quiet picture before any text asks for anything. Phone visitors also get a dense text screen in place of the drawing that defines the look.

findings.where: Title block (nav bar), desktop and phone: the DRAWING MMM-GA-001 and SCALE NTS cells next to PROFILE, ARTICLES, BLOG and CONTACT
findings.fault: The two drawing-reference cells use the same ruled boxes, capitals and colour as the four nav links, and they sit in the same row. By similarity and common region they read as two more menu items, but they do nothing when clicked. On phone they share the top row with the logo while the real links drop to a second row, which makes them look even more like the main controls.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor scanning the bar for where to go. They may click MMM-GA-001 expecting a page, or read the menu as six items when it has four.

findings.where: Phone, texture tile: the EARTH HATCH and POCHE samples inside their framed panel
findings.fault: On phone the panel loses its inner margin. The hatch sample and its label sit flush against the frame's left edge and the poche block against the right edge. The dimension line below collapses into an empty boxed band, so the panel looks broken and not like a drawn specimen. On desktop the same panel has a clear inset.
findings.who_objects: Whoever judges this tile for the layout round, and later Angélique placing images in framed parts. The phone version suggests that framed content crowds its frame at small widths.

findings.where: Phone hero: the name block (circled A marker, MARK M. MOSELEY, role lines) above the blurb and button
findings.fault: The section marker pushes the name and its role lines in to a second left edge at about 83 px, while the blurb and button sit at the page margin of 31 px. Two left edges stack within one screen. The role line also breaks after its bullet, leaving "•" hanging at the line end with SCALE NTS orphaned below.
findings.who_objects: A phone reader. The ragged double edge and the orphaned bullet make the opening block look unsettled, which undercuts the precise, measured drawing-sheet idea.

findings.where: Desktop, bottom of the sheet: the article specimen (left column) beside the motion sketch (right column)
findings.fault: The article column ends with its link card about 220 px above the end of the motion-sketch panel. This leaves an empty block in the lower left before the sheet border, so the closing row looks unfinished and lopsided compared with the balanced rows above it.
findings.who_objects: A reader reaching the end of the sheet. The bottom row looks as if something is missing, which is noticeable on a page whose whole conceit is a carefully composed drawing sheet.

findings.where: Desktop hero drawing: the thin S-curve rising from the ground line on the right, beyond the third arch
findings.fault: A lone hairline climbs from the ground line and stops abruptly at the right content edge, with no label or counterpart on the left. The eye follows it out of the drawing and off the sheet. It pulls the otherwise centred, symmetrical section off balance and reads like a stray stroke rather than terrain.
findings.who_objects: Anyone squinting at the first screen, Mark included. The one calm picture gets an unexplained loose end that draws the eye away from the arches and the name.

findings.where: Phone, motion sketch: the timeline table (ELEMENT, START, LENGTH, EASING)
findings.fault: At phone width the element column wraps each row to three lines ("Daylight falls / through the / third bay"), while the numbers sit beside the first line only. The rows become tall and uneven, and it is hard to tell which values belong to which move.
findings.who_objects: Whoever reads the motion sketch on a phone. The table's job is to show two overlapping moves at a glance, and the wrapped rows hide that.
